1	# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)
2	
3	This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.
4	
5	A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

# Invention disclosure (the inventor's own words)

This is the ONLY authority for what the invention includes. Everything you claim must be supported here or in later messages from the user.

A reusable split pipe clamp has a first semicircular frame half and a second semicircular frame half joined by a hinge at one end and a releasable latch at the other end. Three radial jaw carriages are distributed around the closed frame. Each carriage slides in a radial guide and carries a pivoting concave jaw pad that bears on a pipe without requiring a tool-specific pipe diameter.

A segmented cam ring is retained in an annular guide of the frame. One cam-ring segment is carried by each frame half. When the halves close, complementary drive faces at the hinge and latch ends couple the segments so that they move as one ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the cam ring. Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring and rotates the coupled ring through a limited stroke. The oblique slots translate that rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three jaw carriages. A spring biases each carriage outward when the latch is released.

The latch has a first position that holds the frame halves around the pipe without clamping and a second over-center position that drives the cam ring and clamps the pipe. A force-limiting spring stack lies between the latch handle and the wedge, so additional handle travel after all jaw pads contact the pipe compresses the spring stack rather than forcing one jaw farther than the others. A visible indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing when the spring stack enters a predetermined compression range. The indicator reports clamp loading mechanically and does not measure pipe diameter.

To install the clamp, an operator opens the latch, swings the frame halves apart, places them around a pipe, closes the frame, moves the latch to the holding position, and then moves the latch to the over-center position. The coupled cam ring advances all jaw carriages until the pivoting pads seat on the pipe. To remove the clamp, releasing the latch unloads the spring stack and the carriage springs retract the jaws before the frame halves are opened.

The frame may carry a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, tool, or conduit. The mounting boss does not participate in jaw synchronization. 1	The following description of embodiments refers to the accompanying drawings. The same reference numeral denotes the same part throughout. Terms of direction are used with respect to the frame of the clamp: the axis of the frame is the axis about which the frame is annular in the closed condition, "inward" and "radially inward" mean toward that axis, "outward" and "radially outward" mean away from it, and "circumferential" means about that axis. These terms describe relationships within the clamp and do not require the clamp to be used in any particular attitude.
2	
3	Overall arrangement
4	
5	FIG. 1 shows a split pipe clamp 100 closed around a pipe 90, with the latch 16 in the over-center position described below and the jaw pads 40 seated on the pipe 90. The clamp 100 has a first frame half 10 and a second frame half 12. Each of the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 is semicircular, and the two frame halves together surround the pipe 90. The first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are joined at one end, referred to as the hinge end, by a hinge 14, and are releasably joined at the other end, referred to as the latch end, by a releasable latch 16. The hinge 14 permits the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 to be swung apart far enough for the frame halves to be placed around the pipe 90 from the side. When the frame halves are brought together and the latch 16 is engaged, the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 define a frame that is annular about the axis of the frame.
6	
7	Three jaw carriages 30 are distributed around the frame in the closed condition, so that the three jaw carriages 30 approach the pipe 90 from three different directions. Each jaw carriage 30 moves radially with respect to the frame and carries at its inner end a jaw pad 40, which is described below in connection with FIG. 3. The jaw pads 40 carried at the inner ends of the three jaw carriages 30 bear on the pipe 90 when the clamp 100 is clamped. The clamp 100 does not require a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter, and the same clamp 100 serves pipes of different diameters within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
8	
9	The frame may carry a mounting boss 70 outside the annular guide 18 described below, as shown in FIG. 5, which is a fragmentary view with parts shown in section on a plane containing the axis of the frame and corresponding in orientation to the plane of FIG. 3, that plane passing through the mounting boss 70. The mounting boss 70 supports equipment 80 that is to be held on the pipe 90 by the clamp 100. FIG. 5 shows the equipment 80 supported on the mounting boss 70, the equipment 80 being a sensor, a tool, or a conduit. The mounting boss 70 does not participate in the advance of the three jaw carriages 30 inwardly in synchronism. FIG. 5 also shows the annular guide 18 of the frame with the segmented cam ring 20 received in it, the mounting boss 70 standing outside the annular guide 18, no part of the mounting boss 70 reaching into the annular guide 18. The equipment 80 carried at the mounting boss 70 therefore lies outside the drive path by which the jaws are advanced. The mounting boss 70 is an optional feature of the clamp 100 and may be omitted.
10	
11	The segmented cam ring
12	
13	FIG. 2 shows the segmented cam ring 20, drawn removed from the frame with its segments in the coupled condition. The segmented cam ring 20 comprises a first cam ring segment 22 and a second cam ring segment 24. The first cam ring segment 22 is carried by the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 is carried by the second frame half 12, so that each frame half carries one segment of the ring and each segment travels with its own frame half when the clamp 100 is opened.
14	
15	The first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 meet at two places, one at the hinge end and one at the latch end. At the hinge end the two segments have complementary coupling faces 26, and at the latch end they have complementary coupling faces 28. The complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are each shaped so that one segment can transmit circumferential force to the other through the joint. The faces are brought into engagement by the same motion that closes the frame halves: as the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 are swung together about the hinge 14, the complementary coupling faces 26 close on one another at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 close on one another at the latch end. FIG. 6 shows the joint at the latch end in the closed condition, the end of the first cam ring segment 22 held by the first frame half 10 and the end of the second cam ring segment 24 held by the second frame half 12, the two ends meeting at the complementary coupling faces 28.
16	
17	Coupling the segments in this way solves a problem created by splitting the clamp. Here the division of the ring is undone by the act of closing the clamp. In the closed condition the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 are coupled at both ends and rotate together in the annular guide as a coupled ring, and a circumferential input applied to either segment is carried around the whole ring. One input, applied at one point on one frame half, therefore reaches every jaw carriage 30 through a single kinematic element, and the relationship between the jaw carriages 30 is set by the geometry of the ring rather than by the way the clamp is operated. When the latch 16 is released and the frame halves are swung apart, the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 separate and each segment stays with its own frame half, so that the coupling is made and broken by the closing and opening of the frame halves.
18	
19	The annular guide 18 retains the first cam ring segment 22 on the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 on the second frame half 12, and permits circumferential movement of the coupled ring. Each segment is therefore held on its own frame half whether the clamp 100 is open or closed, and no separate operation is needed to place the ring in the frame when the frame halves are brought together.
20	
21	The segmented cam ring 20 has three oblique slots 34, one for each jaw carriage 30. Each oblique slot 34 is inclined to the radial direction of the frame at the circumferential position of that slot, so that rotation of the coupled ring produces inward travel of its jaw carriage 30, the three oblique slots 34 being arranged so that the three jaw carriages 30 travel inwardly in synchronism.
22	
23	The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch acts as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge moved by the latch can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which that wedge advances, so that advance of the wedge moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
24	
25	The jaw carriages
26	
27	FIG. 3 is a fragmentary sectional view through one jaw carriage 30, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1. The frame is formed with the annular guide 18, which receives the segmented cam ring 20 and holds it against radial movement while leaving it free to move circumferentially.
28	
29	The frame is further formed with a radial guide 38 at the position of each jaw carriage 30, so that the frame in the closed condition has the annular guide 18 and three radial guides 38. Each jaw carriage 30 is received in a respective one of the three radial guides 38 and is constrained by the radial guide 38 to move radially with respect to the frame. Each jaw carriage 30 carries a follower 32 that projects from the jaw carriage 30 into a respective one of the oblique slots 34 of the segmented cam ring 20. The follower 32 bears against the sides of the oblique slot 34.
30	
31	The follower 32 is constrained in two ways at once. The radial guide 38 prevents the jaw carriage 30, and therefore the follower 32, from moving circumferentially, while the oblique slot 34 holds the follower 32 at a position along the slot, which is inclined to the radial direction, so that circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20 displaces the follower 32 radially. When the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the side of each oblique slot 34 bears on the corresponding follower 32 and drives it, and with it the jaw carriage 30, radially inward along the radial guide 38. Because all three followers 32 are engaged in oblique slots 34 of one coupled ring, the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism for as long as the ring turns. The jaw pads 40 therefore close on the pipe together.
32	
33	At its inner end each jaw carriage 30 carries a jaw pad 40. The jaw pad 40 is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage 30 and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. Because the jaw pad 40 is free to pivot on the jaw carriage 30, the concave bearing face aligns itself with the outer surface of the pipe as it lands. The same concave bearing face therefore seats on pipes of different diameters, and no part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter is required.
34	
35	A carriage return spring 44 acts on each jaw carriage 30 so as to urge that jaw carriage 30 radially outward. When the latch 16 is released and the drive from the latch to the ring drive face 36 is removed, the carriage return springs 44 push the jaw carriages 30 outward and the jaw pads 40 are retracted from the pipe, and the clamp 100 is left with its jaw carriages 30 retracted and ready for the next installation. Retraction of the jaw carriages 30 clears the jaw pads 40 from the pipe before the frame halves are swung apart.
36	
37	The latch and the force-limiting drive train
38	
39	The latch 16 includes a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, a wedge 52, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in the drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
40	
41	FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the first cam ring segment 22, the second cam ring segment 24 and the ring drive face 36.
42	
43	The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
44	
45	The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
46	
47	The indicator pin 56 is coupled to the force-limiting spring stack 54 and projects from the latch housing 58. As the force-limiting spring stack 54 compresses, the indicator pin 56 moves relative to a fixed edge of the latch housing 58, and the position of the indicator pin 56 with respect to that fixed edge shows the operator when the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered a predetermined compression range. The indicator pin 56 therefore reports clamp loading mechanically, and what it reports is the state of the force-limiting spring stack 54. The indicator pin 56 is displaced by compression of the force-limiting spring stack 54 independently of a diameter of the pipe 90, and its position is not a measurement of that diameter.
48	
49	Operation
50	
51	To install the clamp 100 on a pipe 90, the operator opens the latch 16 and swings the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 apart about the hinge 14. The first cam ring segment 22 stays with the first frame half 10 and the second cam ring segment 24 stays with the second frame half 12, and the complementary coupling faces 26 and the complementary coupling faces 28 are separated. The operator places the frame halves around the pipe 90 from the side and closes them about the hinge 14. Closing the frame halves brings the complementary coupling faces 26 into engagement at the hinge end and the complementary coupling faces 28 into engagement at the latch end, coupling the first cam ring segment 22 and the second cam ring segment 24 into the coupled ring within the annular guide 18.
52	
53	The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
54	
55	To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.
56	
57	Features described above in connection with one embodiment may be combined with features described in connection with another, except where the context makes the combination impossible. The embodiments described are illustrative of the disclosed clamp and are not exhaustive of it, and the scope of protection is defined by the claims that follow rather than by any particular embodiment described here.

The latch and the force-limiting drive train

A split pipe clamp is disclosed in which the element that advances the gripping jaws is divided with the clamp body but is coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, so that one latch motion advances every jaw together.

In one aspect, a split pipe clamp comprises a first frame half and a second frame half joined at a hinge end by a hinge and releasably joined at a latch end by a latch. In a closed condition the two frame halves define a frame having an annular guide and three radial guides. Three jaw carriages are each slidable radially in a respective one of the radial guides, and each jaw carriage carries a jaw pad that is pivotally mounted on the jaw carriage and has a concave bearing face directed inwardly of the frame. A segmented cam ring is received in the annular guide and comprises a first cam ring segment carried by the first frame half and a second cam ring segment carried by the second frame half. The cam ring segments have complementary coupling faces at the hinge end and complementary coupling faces at the latch end, and those faces engage one another as the frame halves are closed, so that in the closed condition the two segments move in the annular guide as a coupled ring. Each jaw carriage has a follower received in a respective oblique slot of the segmented cam ring, each oblique slot being inclined to a radial direction of the frame so that rotation of the coupled ring through a stroke advances the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism. A wedge movable by the latch bears on a ring drive face of the segmented cam ring, so that movement of the latch rotates the coupled ring through the stroke, and a carriage return spring biases each jaw carriage outwardly so that releasing the latch retracts the jaws.

Because the coupled ring is a single kinematic element spanning both frame halves, the three jaw carriages are not driven independently. One latch motion, applied at one point on one frame half, is distributed by the coupled ring to every jaw carriage, and the jaw pads close on the pipe together. The pivoting concave jaw pads seat on the pipe without a part dimensioned to a particular pipe diameter.

In a further aspect, the latch has a first position in which the frame halves are held around the pipe without clamping and a second, over-center position in which the wedge drives the cam ring and the pipe is clamped, and a force-limiting spring stack lies in the drive train between a latch handle and the wedge. Travel of the handle that remains after all three jaw pads have contacted the pipe compresses the force-limiting spring stack instead of advancing one jaw carriage farther than the others. An indicator pin moves relative to a fixed edge of a latch housing when the force-limiting spring stack enters a predetermined compression range, giving the operator a mechanical report of clamp loading that is produced by the state of the spring stack and not by the diameter of the pipe.

In a further aspect, the frame carries a mounting boss outside the annular guide for supporting a sensor, a tool, or a conduit, the mounting boss not participating in the advance of the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism, so that equipment carried on the frame is outside the path by which the jaws are synchronized.

In a further aspect, a method of clamping a pipe comprises opening the latch, swinging the frame halves apart about the hinge, placing the frame halves around a pipe, closing the frame halves so that the complementary coupling faces engage and couple the cam ring segments, moving the latch to the first position, and moving the latch to the second, over-center position so that the wedge rotates the coupled ring and the followers advance the three jaw carriages inwardly in synchronism until the jaw pads seat on the pipe. Releasing the latch unloads the force-limiting spring stack and the carriage return springs retract the jaw carriages before the frame halves are opened.

1	Equipment is frequently attached to the outside of a pipe after the pipe has been installed. Sensors, small tools, brackets, and lengths of conduit all have to be carried on a pipe that cannot be taken out of service, cannot be lifted, and has no free end over which a closed ring could be threaded. A clamp intended for that duty therefore has to open from the side, close around the pipe, and grip it firmly enough that the carried equipment keeps its position, while remaining removable so that the same clamp can be taken off and used again elsewhere.
2	
3	A clamp that opens from the side is split into parts, and the split is what makes the gripping problem difficult. Once the clamp body is divided, any drive element that runs around the body is divided with it. Gripping arrangements that answer this by driving the gripping surfaces of each part separately give up the fixed relationship between the two parts of the drive: the two sides of the clamp advance by amounts that depend on how each side is operated, so the clamp tends to settle off center on the pipe, and the load is shared unevenly between the gripping surfaces. Arrangements that instead pull the split body closed on the pipe, in the manner of a band or a two-bolt saddle, transfer the closing force through the joint at the split and rely on the pipe itself to react the closing motion, so the grip depends on how nearly the bore of the clamp matches the outside diameter of the pipe. Such an arrangement is commonly supplied with liners or inserts machined for one nominal pipe size, and a different pipe size calls for a different insert or a different clamp.
4	
5	Reusable clamping also has to deal with the force the operator applies. A hand lever gives the operator no measure of what has been done to the pipe. When the gripping elements have reached the pipe, further travel of the lever has to go somewhere, and in a rigid drive train it goes into whichever gripping element happens to touch first, so that one gripping surface is loaded far more than the others. Thin walled tube, coated pipe, and lined pipe are all damaged by that kind of concentrated loading, and the operator has no indication that it has occurred. Torque tools and gauges can be added to the installation, but they add a separate instrument to the task and, when they respond to the position of the gripping elements, they report the size of the pipe rather than the force in the grip.
6	
7	What has been lacking is a split clamp in which the drive that advances the gripping elements is itself coupled by the act of closing the clamp into a single element that moves as one ring, in which every gripping element is advanced from that one drive so that the gripping elements advance together over a range of pipe sizes, and in which the travel remaining in the operator's lever after the gripping elements have landed on the pipe is absorbed within the clamp and reported to the operator as a loading condition rather than as a dimension.
8

reasoning: The reviewer's finding was genuine, not a false positive: claim 1 recites 'a wedge movable by the latch' as an element separate from 'the latch comprising a latch handle and a force-limiting spring stack in a drive train between the latch handle and the wedge'. If the description said the latch 16 includes the wedge 52, then 'the latch' would name two different collections of parts in the two documents, which invites an indefiniteness objection and, worse, an argument that the spring stack sits between the handle and something already inside the latch. I fixed the description rather than the claims because the disclosure itself puts the wedge outside the latch: 'Closing the latch drives a wedge against a drive face of the cam ring.'

I extended the fix one sentence beyond the reviewer's suggestion, into the cam-ring section, because that section was the first place the wedge was named and it named it without a numeral ('the wedge moved by the latch'). Introducing the wedge 52 there follows the rule that a numeral is introduced at the first naming of its part, and it removes a second bare definite article. This changes no structure and adds no new matter; the numerals table already carried 52 for the wedge.

I deliberately kept the claim language unchanged. Claim 1 stands on the combination that the disclosure calls essential: a cam ring split with the frame whose segments are coupled into one rotating ring by the act of closing the frame halves, plus oblique-slot followers that turn that one rotation into synchronized inward travel of all three carriages, plus a force-limiting spring stack that absorbs the latch travel remaining after the pads land. There is no prior art in prior_art/ to write around, so the claim was drawn to the disclosed essential relationship rather than trimmed against any specific reference; if a search later produces art, the coupling-by-closure feature and the spring-stack feature are the two independent places to retreat to, and both already have their own technical problem explained in the specification (the split destroying the fixed relationship between the two sides, and rigid drive trains overloading whichever jaw lands first).

I left the optional mounting boss 70 out of claim 1 and confined it to claim 8 and the assembly claim 10, because the disclosure marks it optional ('The frame may carry...') and expressly says it does not participate in jaw synchronization. Putting it in claim 1 would give away scope for a feature that does no work in the claimed mechanism.

I did not touch the figure briefs. figures/FIG-4.md already draws the wedge 52 as a block in the latch housing cavity with the spring stack 54 between it and the handle 50, which is the relationship the corrected description now states, so the drawings needed no correction and no regeneration on account of this fix. input.prior_art_strategy: prior_art/INDEX.md lists no references ((none) in the key column), so there was nothing to read, nothing that could be cited, and no reference whose vocabulary or teaching had to be written around. The Background accordingly carries no [REF:] citations; adding one would mean inventing a citation. Because no search was run for this draft, the art available here may be incomplete, and the claims have not been tested against any actual reference. The claim set is instead built on the relationship the inventor identifies as essential, and each independent claim recites it in full: the segmented cam ring whose segments are coupled into one rotating ring by the closing of the frame halves themselves, the three oblique slots that convert one limited ring stroke into synchronized inward travel of three radially guided carriages, and the force-limiting spring stack that takes the latch travel remaining after all three pivoting pads have landed. The specification states, before it is needed, the technical problem each of those features solves: splitting the body divides any drive that runs around it, so separately driven sides settle off center and share load unevenly; and a rigid drive train dumps the operator's remaining lever travel into whichever jaw touched first, damaging thin walled, coated and lined pipe with no warning. The dependent ladder gives graduated fallbacks that can each be argued on its own: coupling faces that make and break with the frame halves (claim 7), the annular guide that retains each segment on its own half so no separate assembly step is needed (claim 6), the two-position over-center latch (claims 4 and 12), the indicator pin read against a fixed edge of the latch housing (claims 2 and 11), and the express recitation that the indicator responds to spring-stack compression and not to pipe diameter (claim 3), which is the point that separates this indicator from position-sensing gauges that report size. Independent claims are written in three forms, apparatus, pipe-mounted equipment assembly, and method, so that a clamp maker, an equipment integrator and an installer are each reached.

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary, the other the outer. The three are alike in form and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short flat on the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, just below the right joint: there a single straight edge leaves that boundary at a point spaced from the joint and runs toward the joint, slanting steadily inward so that its end nearer the joint lies radially inside the boundary, cutting a little material from the segment. # FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring alone, removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position and length of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between those two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots below open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26.

At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike in form and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat cut into the outer boundary of the lower segment, the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc running downward from the right joint. The flat has an upper end and a lower end. Its upper end is the end nearer the right joint and lies radially inside the outer boundary, and that upper end stops below the joint, so a short piece of the circular outer boundary runs on from it to the joint. Its lower end is the end further from the right joint and meets the circular outer boundary there. Between those two ends the flat is one straight edge, so the material cut away from the segment is deepest at the upper end and runs out to nothing at the lower end. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts shown in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50 in the over-center position and the manner in which it acts on the force-limiting spring stack 54, the force-limiting spring stack 54 drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting sense of movement of the two bands.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, and at that line the band ends face one another across the parting line along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, so the upper side of that band is exposed. Near the right end of the exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface running between two ends: its left end is the higher and stands at the level of the exposed upper side of the band, and its right end is the lower and lies down within the band, so the surface descends steadily from left to right, that is, toward the parting line. The right end of the ring drive face 36 stops short of the parting line, so a short piece of the exposed upper side runs on from it to that line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36.

A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity above the ring drive face 36. Its lower face is a straight surface descending from left to right at the same slant as the ring drive face 36 and resting on that face along its length, so that downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

Above the wedge 52 the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so that the stack lies between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening left where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position. From that pivot to its outer end it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, which outer surface is the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which the position of the indicator pin 56 is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the descending straight surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

1	# FIG. 6
2	
3	Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame material holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the break running radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.
4	
5	Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.
6	
7	The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the left edge and a further band stands between the channel and the break line.
8	
9	A solid block lies in each channel, filled with its own hatching. Each block is bounded by its own outline, has one long edge facing the left wall of its channel and one long edge facing the right wall, and reaches along its channel to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.
10	
11	At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another, in contact across the full width of the blocks, so the two blocks together fill the parting line where they meet and read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.
12	
13	## Numerals shown on this figure
14	
15	- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band of the upper body between its channel and its left edge.
16	- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band of the lower body between its channel and its left edge.
17	- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band of the upper body between its channel and the break line at the right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
18	- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching well inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.
19	- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching well inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
20	- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the two block end faces at the parting line.

# FIG. 4

Enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, closed, parts in section, viewed along the frame axis from the side opposite that from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top and the circumferential direction runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the latch housing and its cavity, the interruption in the frame wall, the length of the ring drive face 36, the attitude and mounting of the latch handle 50 and the manner in which it acts on the force-limiting spring stack 54, the spring stack drawn as one spring symbol, and the direction in which the wedge 52 advances and the resulting movement of the bands.

At the lower left a hatched body holds a hatched arcuate band from the left; at the lower right a second hatched body holds a like band from the right. The two bodies meet at a parting line, where the band ends face one another along complementary surfaces. The left band is the second cam ring segment 24 and the right band is the first cam ring segment 22.

The frame wall radially outside the left band is interrupted, exposing the upper side of that band. Near the right end of that exposed side the ring drive face 36 is one straight surface: its left end is the higher, at the level of the exposed upper side, and its right end is the lower, down within the band, so the face descends steadily from left to right, toward the parting line. Its right end stops short of that line, a short piece of the exposed upper side running on from it to the line.

Above the parting line a hatched enclosure, the latch housing 58, reaches across both bodies, its left, right and top walls enclosing a cavity that opens downward over the ring drive face 36. A block, the wedge 52, lies in that cavity above the ring drive face 36; its lower face descends from left to right at the same slant and rests on the ring drive face 36 along its length, so downward movement of the wedge 52 presses the left band toward the left.

Above the wedge 52 the force-limiting spring stack 54 is a zigzag line rising from the wedge 52 to the latch handle 50 beside its pivot, so the stack lies between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52.

The latch handle 50 is pivoted to the latch housing 58 at a small circle at the upper right of the cavity and runs up and to the right through an opening where the top and right walls stop short of one another, leaning past upright, the over-center position; from the pivot to its outer end it is a straight bar of even width.

A slender pin, the indicator pin 56, rises from the force-limiting spring stack 54 through a hole in the top wall and projects beyond the outer surface of that wall, which surface is the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 against which the position of the indicator pin 56 is read.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching of the right band.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching of the left band.
- 36 ring drive face: target the descending straight surface on the left band.
- 50 latch handle: target well inside the straight bar.
- 52 wedge: target well inside the block in the cavity.
- 54 force-limiting spring stack: target the zigzag line.
- 56 indicator pin: target the pin above the top wall.
- 58 latch housing: target the hatching of the top wall.

# FIG. 2

Plan view of the segmented cam ring removed from the frame, its two segments coupled, viewed along the ring axis from the same side as FIG. 1, so the hinge end is at the left and the latch end at the right. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the form of the meeting surfaces at the two joints, the positions and tilt of the three slots, and the position and length of the ring drive face 36.

A flat annulus at the centre of the drawing area is the segmented cam ring 20, bounded by one inner circular boundary and one outer circular boundary. The region within the inner boundary is open, and between the two boundaries the face of the ring is flat and unbroken except where the three slots open in it.

Two joints, one at the left and one at the right, divide the annulus into two arcuate segments: the upper is the first cam ring segment 22 and the lower is the second cam ring segment 24.

At the left joint the ends of the two segments meet along complementary surfaces facing circumferentially, the complementary coupling faces at the hinge end 26. At the right joint the two segment ends meet in the same way, the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

Three elongated openings are formed in the annulus, one near the top, one at the lower left, one at the lower right. Each is an oblique slot 34, a long narrow opening lying within the annulus width and inclined to the radius at its own position, so one end is nearer the inner boundary and the other nearer the outer. The three are alike and all tilt the same way: in each, the end nearer the inner boundary lies counterclockwise of the end nearer the outer boundary.

The ring drive face 36 is a short straight flat cut into the outer boundary of the second cam ring segment 24, in the arc running downward from the right joint. Its upper end, the end nearer that joint, lies radially inside the outer boundary and stops below the joint, so a short piece of the circular outer boundary runs on from it to the joint. Its lower end, further from the joint, meets the circular outer boundary. Between the two ends the flat is one straight edge, so the material cut from the segment is deepest at the upper end and runs out to nothing at the lower end. Elsewhere both outer boundaries are circular.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 20 segmented cam ring: target the outer boundary in the upper right.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper segment.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower segment.
- 26 complementary coupling faces at the hinge end: target the surfaces meeting at the left joint.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the surfaces meeting at the right joint.
- 34 oblique slot: target well inside the opening near the top.
- 36 ring drive face: target the straight flat below the right joint.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries hatching of its own at a different slant, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame material holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the break running radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the left edge and a further band between the channel and the break line.

A solid block lies in each channel, bounded by its own outline and filled with its own hatching, one long edge facing the left wall of the channel and one the right wall, and reaching along the channel to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24; the two are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another, in contact across the full width of the blocks, so the two blocks together fill the parting line where they meet and read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the lower body and its left edge.
- 18 annular guide: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and the break line at its right, that band being the wall on the radially outer side of the channel.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the upper body, away from the parting line.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame material holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the break running radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the left edge and a further band stands between the channel and the break line.

A solid block lies in each channel, filled with its own hatching. Each block is bounded by its own outline, has one long edge facing the left wall of its channel and one long edge facing the right wall, and reaches along its channel to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another, in contact across the full width of the blocks, so the two blocks together fill the parting line where they meet and read as one upright body interrupted at the joint. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

## Numerals shown on this figure

- 10 first frame half: target the hatching of the upper body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 12 second frame half: target the hatching of the lower body, clear of the block lying in it.
- 18 annular guide: target the wall of the channel holding the block in the upper body.
- 22 first cam ring segment: target well inside the upper unhatched block.
- 24 second cam ring segment: target well inside the lower unhatched block.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the meeting surfaces at the parting line.

# FIG. 3

Enlarged fragmentary section through one jaw carriage, taken on line 3-3 of FIG. 1, the cutting plane containing that carriage's radial direction and the frame axis, the view's right being the axial side from which FIG. 1 is viewed. Radially outward is toward the top; the axis runs left to right. Cut solid material carries section hatching; black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the carriage return spring 44, the direction in which the annular guide 18 opens, and the way the oblique slot 34 appears as an opening through the segmented cam ring 20.

A hatched body in section spans the upper part of the view, with a groove in its right portion and a channel in its left, the two meeting.

The groove is bounded by the body above and below, closed at its right and open toward the left; its proportions shown schematically. That groove is the annular guide 18.

A hatched block lies in the groove, filling it radially with a small running clearance above and below. That block is the segmented cam ring 20. One short rectangular opening passes through that block from its left face to its right face; apart from that opening the block is solid and hatched throughout, with hatched material above the opening and below it. That opening is the oblique slot 34, its position in the block shown schematically.

The channel runs downward from the groove mouth and opens at the underside of the body. That channel is the radial guide 38.

A hatched block lies in the channel and fills its width, its lower end projecting below the body. That block is the jaw carriage 30. A post extends to the right from its upper end, through the groove mouth and into that opening, its upper and lower sides facing the sides of the opening, so the only open space left in the opening is around the post. That post is the follower 32.

A compression spring drawn as a zigzag line acts between the jaw carriage 30 and the frame body, urging that carriage upward, radially outward. That spring is the carriage return spring 44.

Below the body, a further body hangs from the lower end of the jaw carriage 30 on a small circle, a pivot shown schematically. That body is the jaw pad 40, its lower face a concave arc.

23:The segmented cam ring 20 further has a ring drive face 36, shown in FIG. 2 at the latch end of the ring, against which the latch 16 acts through a wedge 52 as described below. The ring drive face 36 is presented at a position on the ring that the wedge 52 can reach, and it lies at an inclination to the direction in which the wedge 52 advances, so that advance of the wedge 52 moves the segmented cam ring 20 circumferentially.
39:The latch 16 comprises a latch housing 58 at the latch end, a latch handle 50, and a force-limiting spring stack 54 in a drive train between the latch handle 50 and the wedge 52, the wedge 52 being movable by the latch 16. The latch housing 58 presents a fixed edge referred to below in connection with the indicator pin 56. The wedge 52 is positioned so that its inclined face bears on the ring drive face 36 of the segmented cam ring 20.
41:FIG. 4 is an enlarged fragmentary view of the latch end, with parts shown in section, and shows the latch housing 58, the latch handle 50, the wedge 52, the force-limiting spring stack 54 and the indicator pin 56 in their relation to the first cam ring segment 22, the second cam ring segment 24 and the ring drive face 36.
43:The latch 16 has two engaged positions. In a first position, the latch 16 holds the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 closed around the pipe 90 but does not clamp it: the frame is captive on the pipe 90 and cannot fall away, while the segmented cam ring 20 has not yet advanced the jaw carriages 30. In a second, over-center position, the wedge 52 drives the segmented cam ring 20 and the pipe 90 is clamped. Movement of the latch handle 50 from the first position to the second position advances the wedge 52 against the ring drive face 36. The inclined face of the wedge 52 converts that advance into circumferential movement of the segmented cam ring 20, and the coupled ring turns through its limited stroke.
45:The force-limiting spring stack 54 answers the problem of what becomes of the operator's remaining handle travel. The jaw pads 40 land on the pipe 90 at some point in the stroke that depends on the diameter of the pipe 90, and the latch handle 50 has still to be carried into its over-center position. If the drive train from the latch handle 50 to the wedge 52 were rigid, that remaining travel would be taken up by whatever part of the assembly yielded first, in practice by driving one jaw farther into the pipe 90 than the others and loading it far more heavily. Additional travel of the latch handle 50 after all three jaw pads 40 have contacted the pipe 90 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54 rather than forcing one jaw carriage 30 farther inward than the others.
53:The operator then moves the latch 16 to its first position, in which the frame is held around the pipe 90 without clamping. The operator moves the latch handle 50 to the second, over-center position. The wedge 52 is driven against the ring drive face 36, the coupled ring turns through its stroke, the sides of the three oblique slots 34 drive the three followers 32, and the three jaw carriages 30 advance inwardly in synchronism until the pivoting jaw pads 40 seat on the pipe 90. The remaining travel of the latch handle 50 compresses the force-limiting spring stack 54, and the operator watches the indicator pin 56 move relative to the fixed edge of the latch housing 58 and so sees that the force-limiting spring stack 54 has entered the predetermined compression range. The latch 16 is left in the over-center position and the clamp 100 is loaded on the pipe 90.
55:To remove the clamp 100, the operator releases the latch 16. The latch handle 50 comes back over center, the wedge 52 retreats from the ring drive face 36, and the force-limiting spring stack 54 is unloaded. The carriage return springs 44 then push the jaw carriages 30 radially outward, so that the jaw pads 40 lift from the pipe 90. Only then are the first frame half 10 and the second frame half 12 swung apart about the hinge 14 and the clamp 100 taken off the pipe 90. The clamp 100 may be installed again on the same pipe or on a pipe of a different diameter within the radial travel of the jaw carriages 30.

# FIG. 6

Enlarged fragmentary detail of the latch-end joint of the clamp, viewed along the frame axis from the same side as FIG. 1, with the wall of the frame nearest the viewer broken away over the region shown so that the ends of the two cam ring segments are visible. Here the circumferential direction of the frame runs vertically and radially outward is toward the right. The view is confined to the two frame ends at this joint and the two segment ends. Cut frame material carries section hatching, and each segment end carries section hatching of its own at a slant different from that of the frame hatching, so that each segment end reads as a solid body distinct from the frame material holding it. Black line work on white, well inside the drawing area. Shown schematically: the extent of the region, the proportions of the bodies, the form of the meeting surfaces, and the break running radially outward short of the frame wall interrupted in FIG. 4.

Two hatched bodies stand one above the other, one filling the upper part of the view and one the lower part, with a parting line between them running the full width of the view. The upper body is the latch end of the first frame half 10 and the lower body is the latch end of the second frame half 12. Each body is bounded on the left by an upright edge, on the right by an irregular break line, and toward the parting line by a straight horizontal end face reaching from its left edge to its right.

The annular guide 18 of each frame half appears as a channel opening toward the parting line, one in the upper body opening downward and one in the lower body opening upward. Each channel is set back from the left edge of its body and from the break line at its right, so a band of hatched frame material stands between the channel and the left edge and a further band stands between the channel and the break line.

A solid block filled with its own hatching lies in each channel, one long edge facing the left wall of its channel and one long edge facing the right wall, and reaches along its channel to the end face of its body without passing beyond it. The block in the upper body is the first cam ring segment 22 and the block in the lower body is the second cam ring segment 24. The two blocks are of the same width and stand in line.

At the parting line the lower end face of the first cam ring segment 22 and the upper end face of the second cam ring segment 24 lie against one another, in contact across the full width of the blocks, so the two blocks together fill the parting line where they meet. Those surfaces in contact are the complementary coupling faces at the latch end 28.

- 10 first frame half: target the hatched band between the channel of the upper body and its left edge.

- 24 second cam ring segment: target the hatching inside the block in the lower body, away from the parting line.
- 28 complementary coupling faces at the latch end: target the horizontal contact between the end faces of the two blocks at the parting line.

input.summary: Every failing sheet was repaired by strengthening the figure brief so the renderer has an unambiguous, positively stated geometry to draw, and by trimming invented rendering constraints. No claim, no line of the description, no numeral definition and no disclosed embodiment was altered to accommodate anything a generated image drew. FIG. 1: the pipe 90 is now stated to appear as one circle with the area within it blank, and the ring-shaped space between the pipe 90 and the inner circle of the frame body is stated to be open, crossed only by the jaw pads 40 and the inner ends of the jaw carriages 30, which removes the doubled contour the renderer produced; the hinge 14 is now positively confined to the width of the annular frame body between the inner and outer circles, so the oversized housing that was drawn outboard of the ring has no basis in the brief. FIG. 2: the ring drive face 36 is now given both of its ends explicitly, the upper end nearer the right joint lying radially inside the outer boundary and stopping below the joint with a short piece of circular boundary running on to the joint, the lower end further from the joint meeting the circular boundary, so the flat can only be drawn deepening toward the joint and not the reverse. FIG. 4: the same face is described by its two ends in that view, left end high at the level of the exposed upper side of the band and right end low within the band, so it descends from left to right toward the parting line, and the wedge 52 is described as resting on it along its length at the same slant, which is what makes downward movement of the wedge press the band toward the left. FIG. 6: the two segment ends are now drawn as solid blocks carrying hatching of their own at a slant different from the frame hatching, each bounded by its own outline within its channel, so they can no longer read as empty channel space; the two end faces are stated to lie against one another in contact across the full width of the blocks at the parting line, closing the gap that was drawn; and the leader targets were separated, 10 and 12 to the hatched band between each channel and its left edge, 18 to the hatched band between the upper channel and the break line at its right, 22 and 24 to the hatching inside their blocks away from the parting line, and 28 to the horizontal contact between the two block end faces, which also gives 28 a real feature to land on now that the faces touch. Alongside these fixes the briefs were shortened by removing rendering controls that were not disclosure geometry, including the prescription that the latch handle be one bar with two straight parallel long edges and a square-closed end, the hatch-placement instruction above and below the slot opening in FIG. 3, and several restatements of proportions. Numerals per sheet are unchanged and still 8, 7, 8, 8, 4 and 6, the union is still the 26 numerals in draft/numerals.md, and the line 3-3 chain across figures/FIG-1.md, figures/FIG-3.md, draft/07-drawings.md and draft/08-detailed-description.md is untouched.
reasoning: The FIG. 2 and FIG. 4 findings pointed at the same physical surface seen from two sides, so I checked the kinematics before rewriting rather than simply matching each brief to its own picture. With the wedge above the band and descending, the contact force on the band runs into the band along the normal of the inclined face; for the band to be driven to the left in FIG. 4 the face must be higher at its left end and lower at its right end. That is what the brief already required and what the renderer contradicted, so the invention text stayed put and the brief was made explicit by naming both ends of the face instead of relying on the phrase slanting down to the right, which the image model read backwards.

The two briefs also have to agree with one another across a mirror. FIG. 4 is viewed from the side opposite FIG. 1, so its left band is the second cam ring segment 24; mapping FIG. 4's leftward push back into the FIG. 2 view puts the ring stroke clockwise there, which is the sense that carries each follower toward the inner end of its oblique slot given the slot handedness FIG. 2 already specifies. Describing the drive face in FIG. 2 by its upper and lower ends, deepest at the end nearer the latch joint, keeps that agreement and rules out the rendered version that started at the joint and ran away from it.

For FIG. 6 the renderer read the segment ends as voids because the brief asked for unhatched outlines inside a hatched frame. The cure is a drawing convention, not a change to the invention: the segment ends now carry hatching at a slant different from the frame hatching and each block is bounded by its own outline inside its channel, so the block reads as a solid held in the guide. Nothing about the cam ring in the claims or the description changed, and the convention is stated in the brief where it belongs.

The shared endpoints for 18 and 22 were a consequence of the geometry itself, since the annular guide is a groove in the frame half and the segment sits inside it, so any target on the groove wall sits next to the block. I separated them by naming three different bodies of material across the width of the view: the hatched band on the left of the channel for the frame half, the hatched band between the channel and the break line for the annular guide, and the hatching inside the block for the segment. The missing 28 leader followed from the drawn gap; with the end faces stated to be in contact, the coupling faces exist as a feature that a leader can reach.

I resisted the temptation to soften the invention to fit the pixels. The blocks meeting in contact at the parting line is the disclosed coupling that makes the two segments move as one ring, and it is what claim 1 and claim 13 recite; a drawn gap is a rendering defect, so the brief was tightened to demand contact rather than the text loosened to permit a gap.
